translations.text: After Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, the Israelites asked the Lord, “Who will go up first for us against the Canaanites to fight them in battle?”
The Lord said, “Judah will go up. Look, I have handed the land over to him.”
Judah said to his brother Simeon, “Come up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight the Canaanites. I will also go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went, and the Lord handed the Canaanites and the Perizzites over to them. They killed ten thousand of their men at Bezek.
They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek, fought against him, and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
The lord of Bezek fled, but they pursued him, captured him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes.

The lord of Bezek said, “Seventy kings whose thumbs and big toes had been cut off used to gather bread from under my table. God has repaid me just as I did to them.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The people of Judah fought against Jerusalem, captured it, struck it with the sword, and burned its villages with fire.
Afterward, the people of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, the south, and the plain.
Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron. Hebron was formerly named Kiriath-arba. They killed Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, descendants of the giants.
From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. Debir was formerly named Kiriath-sepher.
Caleb said, “Whoever captures Kiriath-sepher and destroys it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife.
As she was coming in, she wanted to ask her father for a field. She got down from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, “What is it, my daughter?”
She said to him, “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me land in the south, give me a source of water.” Caleb gave her the upper water source and the lower water source.
The descendants of Cain, Moses' father-in-law, went up from the City of Palms with the people of Judah into the wilderness of Judah south of Arad. They went and settled the people there.
Simeon went with his brother Judah, and they struck down the Canaanites who lived in Zephath and destroyed it completely. They named the town Hormah.
Judah captured Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, and Ekron and its territory.
The Lord was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country. But they did not destroy the inhabitants of the valley, because they had iron chariots.
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he killed and wiped out the three descendants of the giants there.
The people of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem. The Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
The house of Joseph also went up to Bethel, and the Lord was with them.
The house of Joseph spied out Bethel. The town was formerly named Luz.
The scouts saw a man coming out of the town and said to him, “Show us where the entrance to the town is, and we will make peace with you.”
He showed them the entrance to the town, and they struck the town with the sword. But they spared that man and his entire family.
The man went to the land of the Hittites, built a town, and named it Luz. That is the town’s name to this day.

Manasseh did not destroy Beth-shean and its villages, Taanach and its villages, the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages. The Canaanites who lived in that land were not subdued.
When Israel grew strong, it subjected the Canaanites to tribute, but it did not destroy them completely.
Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, and the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer.
Zebulun did not destroy the inhabitants of Kitron or the inhabitants of Nahalol, and the Canaanites lived with them and were subjected to tribute.
Asher did not destroy the inhabitants of Acco or the inhabitants of Sidon, or Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob.
The Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, because they did not destroy them.

Naphtali did not destroy the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh or the inhabitants of Beth-anath. They lived among the Canaanites who inhabited the land, and the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath were subjected to tribute to them.
The Amorites drove the Danites back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the valley.
The Amorites persisted in living in the land of Heres, on the mountain, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim; but the hand of the house of Joseph grew strong, and they were subjected to tribute.
The border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock and upward.

The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said to the Israelites: "Thus says the Lord: I brought you up from the land of Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers, and I said that I would never break my covenant with you.
And you were not to make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you were to tear down their altars. But you did not listen to my voice. Why have you done this?
So I also have said: I will not drive them out before you; they will become a vexation [?] to you, and their gods will be a stumbling block to you."
When the angel of the Lord spoke all these words to Israel, all the people lifted up their voices and wept.
The people named that place Bochim, and they offered sacrifice there to the Lord.
Joshua dismissed the people, and the Israelites went each to his own inheritance to take possession of the land.
The people served the Lord all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen the works of the Lord and the great deeds he had done for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten years.
They buried him within the border of his inheritance at Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
That whole generation also was gathered to their fathers, and another generation arose after them that did not know the Lord, nor the works he had done for Israel.
The Israelites did what was evil before the Lord and served Baal.

They forsook the Lord, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, and went after other gods, gods of the peoples around them, and worshiped them, and provoked the Lord to anger.
They forsook the Lord and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.

The Lord was angry with Israel, and he handed them over to plunderers who plundered them, and he handed them over to their enemies around them, so that they could no longer stand before their enemies.
Wherever they went out, the hand of the Lord was against them for harm, as the Lord had said and as the Lord had sworn to them, and they were in great distress.
Then the Lord raised up judges in the house of Israel, and they rescued them from the hand of their plunderers.

Yet they would not listen even to their judges, because they went astray after other gods and worshiped them. They quickly turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked in obedience to the commandments of the Lord; they did not do so.

When the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judges and rescued them from the hands of their enemies throughout the judges’ lives. The Lord heard their groaning because of those who oppressed and harassed them.
When the judges died, they turned back and became more corrupt than their ancestors, following other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not give up their deeds or their evil ways.
The Lord became angry with Israel and said, “Because this people has broken my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors to keep, and has not obeyed my voice,
I too will no longer destroy before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died.”
This was so that through them the Lord might test Israel, to see whether they would keep the Lord’s way and walk in it as their ancestors had kept it, or not.
The Lord left these nations and did not destroy them quickly, nor did the Lord hand them over to Joshua.
These are the nations the Lord left to test Israel through them—all those who had not experienced any of the wars against the Canaanites.
This was only so that the generations of the Israelites might know and learn warfare; only the earlier generations had not known it.

The five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon, and from the mountain of the sons of Hermon as far as the entrance to Hamath.
They were there to test Israel, to find out whether they would obey the Lord’s commandments, which he had commanded their ancestors through Moses.
The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hivites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hittites, and Jebusites.
They took their daughters as wives for themselves and gave their own daughters to their sons.
They served their gods. The Israelites did what was evil before the Lord, forgot the Lord their God, and served Baal and the Ashtoreths.
The Lord became angry with Israel and handed them over to Cushan the Wicked, king of Aram-naharaim. The Israelites served Cushan the Wicked for eight years.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for the Israelites, who rescued them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
The hand of the Lord was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to battle, and the Lord handed Cushan the Wicked, king of Aram-naharaim, over to him. His hand prevailed over Cushan the Wicked.
The land had rest for forty years, and Othniel son of Kenaz died.
The Israelites again did what was evil before the Lord, and the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel because they had done what was evil before the Lord.
He gathered the Ammonites and Amalek against them. They went and defeated Israel and took possession of the City of Palms.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

The Israelites cried out to the Lord, and the Lord raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin, a man whose right hand was disabled. The Israelites sent tribute through him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a double-edged sword, a [?] in length, and strapped it beneath his clothing on his right thigh.
He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. King Eglon was a very fat man.
When he had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried it.

He himself turned back from the idols beside Gilgal and said to him, “I have a secret message to tell you, O king, between you and me.” The king said, “Go away from there,” and all those standing beside him withdrew.
Ehud came in to him while he was sitting alone in the upstairs room that had been prepared for him. Ehud said to him, “I have a message from God to tell you.” Eglon rose from his throne.
Ehud reached out his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and struck him in the belly.
The hilt went in after the thrust, and the fat closed over the wound, because he did not pull the sword out of his belly. Then he hurried out.
Ehud [?] went out into the portico, closed the door of the upper room behind him, and left.
After he went out, the servants came in and saw that the doors of the upper room were shut. They said, “Perhaps he has gone to relieve himself in the inner chamber of the upper room.”
They waited a long time and saw that he had not opened the doors of the upper room. They took the keys and opened them, and saw their master lying dead on the floor.
While they were wondering what to do, Ehud passed beyond the idols, escaped, and ran to Seirah.
When he arrived, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down from the hills with him, and he was at their head.
He said to them, “Follow me, because the Lord has handed your enemies, the Moabites, over to you.” They went down after him and seized the Jordan crossings leading to Moab, and they let no one cross.
At that time they killed about ten thousand Moabite men, all wealthy and all powerful warriors. Not one escaped.
So the Moabites were crushed under Israel’s hand at that time, and the land was at peace for eighty years.
After him came Shamgar son of Anath. He struck down six hundred Philistine men with an oxgoad, and he too delivered Israel.
The Israelites again did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and Ehud [?] died.
The Lord handed them over to Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Nations.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord, because he had nine hundred iron chariots and had oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.
Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.
Deborah used to sit under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went up to her for judgment.

She sent for Barak son of Abinoam from Rekem in Naphtali and said to him, “Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you to go and take up a position on Mount Tabor, taking ten thousand men with you from the people of Naphtali and Zebulun?
They will come with you to the Kishon River against Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, and against his chariots and his army, and I will hand him over to you.”
Barak said to her, “If you go with me, I will go. But if you do not go with me, I will not go.”

She said to him, "I will certainly go with you. But, Barak, you will not gain glory from the journey you are taking, because the Lord will hand Sisera over to a woman." Deborah got up and went with Barak to Rekem.
Barak gathered Zebulun and Naphtali at Rekem. Ten thousand men went up with him, and Deborah also went up with him.
Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, from the descendants of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, and pitched his tent as far away as the terebinth at Zaanannim, beside Rekem.
Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor.
Sisera gathered all his chariots—nine hundred iron chariots—and all the troops with him, from Harosheth of the Nations to the Kishon River.
Deborah said to Barak, “Get up! This is the day when the Lord has handed Sisera over to you. Look, the Lord has gone out ahead of you!” So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men.
The Lord crushed Sisera, all his chariots, and his entire army by the sword before Barak. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak pursued his chariots and his army as far as Harosheth of the Nations. Sisera's entire army fell by the sword, and no one escaped alive.
Sisera fled on foot and entered the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and Heber the Kenite.
Jael went out to meet Sisera and said to him, “Come in, my lord, come in here with me. Do not be afraid.” He went into her tent, and she covered him with a blanket.
He said to her, “Please give me a little water to drink, because I am thirsty.” She opened a skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him.
He said to her, “Stand at the entrance of the tent. If anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is anyone here?’ tell him, ‘No.’”

Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg and held a hammer in her hand. She went in to him while he was sleeping, drove the peg into his temple, and drove it into the ground. He was asleep and exhausted, and he died.

Barak was pursuing Sisera, and Jael went out to meet him. She said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” He went in with her and saw Sisera lying dead, with the peg in his temple.
On that day the Lord crushed Jabin, king of Canaan, before the Israelites.
The Israelites’ power continued to grow stronger against Jabin, king of Canaan, until they killed Jabin, king of Canaan.
On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang praise, saying:
“For the vengeance that Israel received, for the praise of the people, praise the Lord!
Listen, kings! Pay attention, rulers! I will praise the Lord and sing to him, to the Lord, the God of Israel.
Lord, when you went out from Seir, when you marched through the fields of Edom, the earth shook, the heavens dripped, and the clouds sprinkled water.
The mountains shook before the Lord, and this Sinai shook before the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, and in the days of Jael, the roads were deserted. Those who had traveled along straight paths traveled along winding roads.
The open settlements of Israel were deserted; they were deserted until I, Deborah, arose, until I arose as a mother in Israel.
He will choose a new god, and then barley bread. Neither sword nor spear will be seen among forty thousand in Israel.
My heart speaks to the heralds of Israel, those who are distinguished among the people: bless the Lord!
You who ride white donkeys, who sit in houses, and who travel along the roads,

reflect on the words of those who dispute among the teachers. There they will recount the Lord’s righteousness, the righteousness he displayed abundantly in Israel. Then the Lord’s people went down to the gate.
Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, give thanks, and speak a song of praise! Arise, Barak, and take your captives captive, son of Abinoam!
Then a deliverer came down to give praise before the Lord, who came down for me as a warrior.
From Ephraim and his servants in Amalek; after you, Benjamin, in your love. From Machir a herald came out, and from Zebulun those who write with a scribe’s pen.
The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah, and Issachar, like Barak, was sent among the peoples at his feet. For the divisions of Reuben there were great searches of the heart.
Why do you sit among the paths, listening to the whistling of wild donkeys? For the division of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.
Gad dwelt beyond the Jordan, and Dan stayed at the harbor of the ships. Asher sat on the seashore and dwelt by its inlets.
Zebulun was a people who scorned their lives to the point of death, and Naphtali was on the heights of its fields.
Kings came and fought. Then the kings of Canaan gathered; they gathered at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. They took no possessions or silver.
The stars fought from their places; from heaven they fought against Sisera.
He swept them away in the Kishon stream, the Kishon stream and the stream of [?]. My soul, tread down strength!
Then the hooves of his horses fell at the thundering force of his mighty warriors.
‘Curse Meroz,’ said the angel of the Lord. ‘Curse it, and curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to the Lord’s aid among the warriors.’
Blessed among women be Jael [?], the wife of Heber the Kenite; blessed be she among women who live in tents.
He asked for water, and she gave him milk; in a warriors’ bowl she offered cream.
She stretched out her hand to the tent peg, and her right hand to the carpenter’s hammer. She struck Sisera and crushed his head; she struck and pierced his temple.
Between her feet he sank down, fell, and lay still. Where he sank down, there he fell, stripped.
Sisera’s mother looked out through the window and cried out through the lattice, saying, “Why is my son’s chariot so late in coming? Why is the axle of his chariot delayed?”
The wisest of her young women also answered and said to her:

“Perhaps he has gone and found abundant plunder and is dividing it: a mule, a mule for each man, and abundant plunder, dyed fabrics and embroidered cloth for Sisera, and dyed fabrics and embroidered cloth for the necks of the plunderers.”
So may all your enemies perish, Lord! But may those who love you be like the sun rising in its strength. And the land was at peace for forty years.
The Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord handed them over to the Midianites for seven years.
The Midianites’ power grew strong over Israel, and the Israelites fled from the Midianites and made homes for themselves in the mountains, along with caves and strongholds.
Whenever Israel sowed, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the people of Rekem would come up.
They would camp against them and devastate the whole land as far as the entrance to Gaza. They would not allow Israel to keep cattle, sheep, or donkeys alive.
For they would come with their livestock and their tents, as numerous as locusts. They and their camels were beyond counting, and they entered the land to devastate it.
Israel was greatly shaken by the Midianites.
The Israelites cried out to the Lord because of Midian.
The Lord sent a prophet to the Israelites, and he said to them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up from the land of Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.
I rescued you from the power of the Egyptians and from the power of all your oppressors. I destroyed them before you and gave you their land.
I said to you, ‘I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you live.’ But you did not obey my voice.”
The angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the terebinth in Ophrah, the town of Joash, Ezri's father. His son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to escape from the Midianites.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him and said to him, “The Lord is with you, mighty warrior.”

Gideon said to him, “Please, my lord, if the Lord is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about, saying, ‘The Lord brought us out of Egypt’? But now the Lord has abandoned us and handed us over to the Midianites.”
The Lord turned toward him and said to him, “Go in this strength of yours, and you will save Israel from the power of the Midianites. Look, I have sent you.”
He said to him, “Please, my lord, how can I save Israel? Look, my clan is insignificant in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s household.”
The Lord said to him, "I will be with you, and you will defeat the Midianites as though they were one man."
He said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, give me a sign so that I may know that it is you who are speaking with me.
Do not leave here until I come back to you and bring out my meal and set it before you.” He said, “I will stay until you return.”

Gideon went inside and prepared a young goat and unleavened bread from a seah of flour. He put the meat in a basket and poured the broth into a pot. He brought it out to him beneath the terebinth and presented it to him.
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread and put them on the rock, and pour the broth over it.” And he did so.

The angel of the Lord reached out with the tip of the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire rose from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread, and the angel of the Lord disappeared from his presence.
Gideon realized that he was the angel of the Lord, and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord God! I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face!”
The Lord said to him, “Peace be with you. Do not be afraid; you will not die.”
Gideon built an altar to the Lord there and called it "The Lord Is Peace." To this day it is still in Ophrah, the town of Ezri's father.
That day the Lord said to him, “Take your father’s bull and another bull, seven years old. Tear down the altar of Baal, your father’s idol, and cut down the Asherah pole standing above it.

Build an altar to the Lord your God on top of this stronghold, arranging it properly. Take the other bull and offer it on the altar as a burnt offering, with wood [?] from the Asherah pole that you cut down.”
Gideon took ten men from among his servants and did as the Lord had told him. Because he was afraid of his father’s household and the men of the town, he did it at night rather than by day.

The men of the town rose early in the morning and saw that Baal’s altar had been torn down, the Asherah pole above it had been cut down, and the other bull had been offered on another altar that had been built.
They said to one another, “Who did this?” They asked questions and investigated, and they said, “Gideon son of Joash did this.”
The men of the town said to Joash, “Bring out your son so that he may die, because he tore down Baal’s altar and cut down the Asherah pole above it.”

Joash said to everyone standing against him, “Will you plead Baal’s case? Will you save him? Whoever pleads his case must die by morning. If he is a god, let him plead his own case, because someone has torn down his altar.”
That day he named him Jerubbaal, saying, “Let Baal bring a case against him, because he tore down his altar.”
All the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the people of Rekem gathered together, crossed over, and camped in the valley of Jezreel.
The Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon. He blew the trumpet and summoned Jezreel to follow him.
He sent his messengers throughout Manasseh, and they too rallied behind him. He also sent his messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
Gideon said to the Lord, “If you are going to save Israel through me, as you have said,
look, I am putting a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, while all the ground is dry, I will know that you are going to save Israel through me, as you have said.”
And that is what happened. He rose early the next day and wrung out the fleece, squeezing from it enough dew to fill a bowl with water.

Gideon said to God, “Do not let your anger burn against me. Let me speak just this once more. Let me make one more test with the fleece: let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be dew on all the ground.”
God did so that night. The fleece alone was dry, and there was dew on all the ground.
Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, rose early with all the people who were with him, and they camped beside the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Ramah, in the valley.
The Lord said to Gideon, “The people with you are too many for me to hand the Midianites over to you. Otherwise Israel might boast and say, ‘My own hand has given me victory.’”
Now proclaim within the people's hearing, "Whoever is afraid and trembling may leave and return from Mount Gilead." Twenty-two thousand of the people returned, and ten thousand remained.

The Lord said to Gideon, “There are still too many people. Bring them down to the water, and I will test them for you there. Whoever I tell you is to go with you shall go with you, and whoever I tell you is not to go with you shall not go with you.”

He brought the people down to the water, and the Lord said to Gideon, “Put together in one group everyone who laps the water with his tongue as a dog laps, and put together in another group everyone who kneels down to drink.”
The number of those who lapped, bringing their hands to their mouths, was three hundred men. All the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.

The Lord said to Gideon, “Through these three hundred men who lap water by bringing their hands to their mouths, I will save you and hand the Midianites over to you. Let all the other people go, each to his own place.”

All the people took their provisions in their hands, along with their horns. He dismissed all the Israelites, each to his own property and his tent, and retained the three hundred men as his force. The camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
That night the Lord said to him, “Get up and go down to the camp, because I have handed it over to you.”
“If you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.”
“You will hear what they are saying, and then your hands will be strengthened.” So he went down to the camp with Purah his servant, to the head of the fifty men in the camp.
Midian, Amalek, and all the people of Rekem were encamped in the valley, as numerous as locusts. They and their camels were beyond counting, as numerous as the sand on the seashore.

Gideon arrived and saw a man telling his companion a dream. He said to him, “In my dream I saw a loaf of barley bread tumbling through the camp of Midian. It reached a tent and overturned it, and the tent fell.”
His companion answered him, “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the warrior of Israel. God has handed the camp of Midian over to him.”

When Gideon heard the account of the dream and its interpretation, he bowed down in worship. He returned to the camp of Israel and said, “Get up, because the Lord has handed the camp of Midian over to you!”
He divided the three hundred men into three companies. He put horns into the hands of all of them, along with empty jars and torches inside the jars.
He said to them, “Watch me and do the same. Look, I am going into the camp. Do just as I do.”
“When I blow the trumpet, I and all the people with me, you too must blow the trumpet all around the camp and say, ‘A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!’”
Gideon and the hundred men with him entered the edge of the camp during the middle watch, just after the guards had been posted.

The three hundred leaders blew the horns and broke the jars. They held the torches in their left hands and the horns in their right hands to blow them, and shouted, “A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!”
They stood, each in his place, around the camp. The whole camp ran, crying out and fleeing.

The three hundred horns sounded, and the Lord turned each man’s sword against his companion throughout the camp. The whole camp fled as far as Beth-shittah and Zeredah, and as far as the border of Abel-meholah, beside Tabbath.
The Israelites from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh were called out, and they pursued Midian.

Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim, saying, “Come down to meet Midian and seize the waterways as far as Beth-barah beside the Jordan.” All the men of Ephraim were called out, and they seized the waterways as far as Beth-barah on the Jordan.

They captured the two leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock, and they killed Zeeb at Beth-Qabrab [?]. They pursued Midian and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan.
The people of Ephraim said to him, "Why did you do this and not call us when you went to fight against Midian?" They argued bitterly with him.
He said to them, “What have I done now to compare with you? Was not Ephraim’s gleaning better than the grape harvest of Jezreel—and in Jezreel [?]?”
“God handed the two leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. What have I been able to do to compare with you?” Then their anger toward him subsided when he said this.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed it with the three hundred men who were with him, running and exhausted.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Give a loaf of bread to each of the people with me, because they are exhausted. I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
The leaders of Succoth said to him, “Are Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hands, that we should give bread to your army?”
Gideon said to them, “Because of this, when the Lord hands Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I will thresh your flesh on the thorns and briers of the wilderness.”
He went up from there to Penuel, and the men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had.
He also said to the men of Penuel, "When I return safely, I will tear down this tower."

Zebah and Zalmunna were encamped at Qarqab [?], with their armies, about fifteen thousand men—all who remained of all the armies of the people of the east. One hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had fallen.
Gideon went up by the road of the tent dwellers, east of [?] and Jogbehah, and struck the army while the army was at ease.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and they pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, throwing the whole army into panic.
Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Hadas.
He captured a young man from among the men of Succoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for him the leaders of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

He came to the men of Succoth and said to them, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are Zebah and Zalmunna bound in your hands, that we should give bread to your exhausted servants?’”
He dragged the elders of the town over desert thorns and briers, and with these he tortured the men of Succoth.
He tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the town.
He said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “Where are the men you killed at Tabor?” They said to him, “They were like you, looking like sons of a king.”
He said, “They were my brothers, my mother’s sons. As the Lord God lives, if you had kept them alive, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether, his firstborn, “Get up and kill them.” But the boy did not draw his sword, because he was afraid, since he was still a boy.

Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up yourself and strike us down, for a man’s strength matches the man.” Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the crescent ornaments that were on their camels’ necks.
The Israelites said to Gideon, “Rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson—for you have saved us from the power of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you. The Lord will rule over you.”
Gideon said to them, “I ask one thing of you: each of you, give me an earring from his plunder.” For they had gold earrings, because they were Arabs.
They said to him, “We will give them to you.” He spread out a cloak, and each man threw an earring from his plunder onto it.

The weight of the gold earrings he requested was seventeen hundred in gold, apart from the crescent ornaments, necklaces, and purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and apart from the necklaces on their camels’ necks. Gideon took these from them.
He made a [?] and set it up in his town, Ophrah. The Israelites went astray after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household.
The Midianites were defeated before the Israelites and never again raised their heads. The land was at peace for forty years during Gideon’s lifetime.
Jerubbaal [?] son of Joash went and lived in his house.
Gideon had seventy sons of his own, for he had many wives.
His concubine in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the town of his father Joash, in Ophrah of Abiezer.
When Gideon died, the Israelites turned back and went astray after Baal, and made Baal-berith their god.
The Israelites did not remember the Lord their God, who delivered them from all their enemies around them.
They did not show kindness to the household of [?], that is, Gideon, in keeping with all the kindness he had shown Israel.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal [?] went to Shechem, to his mother’s brothers, and spoke to them and to the whole clan of his mother’s father’s household.

He said before all the leaders of Shechem, “Which is better for you: for seventy men, the sons of Jerubbaal [?], to rule over you, or for one man to rule over you? Remember that I am your own flesh and bone.”
His mother's brothers spoke all these words about him before all the leaders of Shechem. Their hearts inclined toward Abimelech, and they said, “He is our brother.”
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith. With these Abimelech hired worthless, reckless men, who followed him.
He went into his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham, Jerubbaal's youngest son, survived because he had hidden himself.
All the leaders of Shechem and all the people of Beth-millo gathered together. They went and made Abimelech king over them beside the oak of the watchtower in Shechem.
When Jotham was told, he went up and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim. He raised his voice and said, “Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.
“The trees went out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
The olive tree said to them, "I will not give up my oil, through which gods and people are honored, and go sway over the trees."
The trees said to the fig tree, ‘Come, you reign over us.’
The fig tree said to them, "I will not give up my sweetness and my good fruit and go sway over the trees."
The trees said to the vine, "You come and reign over us."
The vine said to them, ‘I will not leave my [?], which gladdens the hearts of gods and people, and go to sway over the trees.’
All the trees said to the thornbush, ‘You reign over us.’
The thornbush said to the trees, ‘If you are truly anointing me to reign over you, come and take shelter in my shade. Otherwise, let fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’
“Now, if you have acted honestly and faithfully in making Abimelech king, and if you have treated Jerubbaal and his household well, or have repaid him according to the work of his hands—
for my father fought for you, risked his life in battle, and rescued you from the power of Midian—

yet today you have risen against my father's household and killed his sons, seventy men, on one stone. You have made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your brother.
If, then, you have acted honestly and faithfully today toward Jerubbaal's family and his household, rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.

Otherwise, let fire come out of Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and the leaders of Millo. And let fire come out from among the leaders of Shechem and the leaders of Millo and consume Abimelech.”
Jotham fled and escaped. He went to Debir and lived there, where Abimelech had lived previously.
Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
God sent an evil spirit upon Abimelech and upon the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech.

This was so that the wrong done to Jerubbaal's seventy sons might come back upon their brother Abimelech, who had killed them, and their blood be laid upon him and upon the leaders of Shechem, who had strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
They set men in ambush against him on the mountaintop, and they robbed everyone who passed them on the road. Abimelech was told about this.
Gaal son of Epher came with his brothers and passed through Shechem. The leaders of Shechem put their trust in him.
They went out into the fields, harvested their vineyards, pressed the grapes, and held a celebration. They entered the temple of their gods, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Epher said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his deputy? Serve the men of Hamor, Shechem's father! Why should we serve him?
If only someone would put this people into my hands! Then I would remove Abimelech.” He said to Abimelech, “Increase your army and come out!”
Zebul, the ruler of the town, heard the words of Gaal son of Epher, and his anger flared up.
He deceitfully sent messengers to Abimelech, saying, “Look, Gaal son of Epher and his brothers have come to Shechem, and they are surrounding the city to oppose you.
Now get up during the night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush in the open country.
In the morning, when the sun rises, get up and advance against the city. When he and the people with him come out against you, do to them whatever you can.”
Abimelech and all the people with him got up during the night and lay in ambush against Shechem in four companies.
Gaal son of Epher went out and stood at the entrance to the city gate, and Abimelech and the people with him rose from their ambush.
Gaal saw the people and said to Zebul [?], “Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!” Zebul [?] said to him, “You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as though they were people.”
Gaal spoke again and said to Zebul [?], “Look, people are coming down from the high ground, and one company is coming along the road by the oak of Meonenim.”
Zebul [?] said to him, “Where is that mouth of yours that used to say, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?’ Are these not the people you despised? Go out now and fight them.”
Gaal went out at the head of the city's leaders and fought against Abimelech.
Abimelech pursued him, and he fled before him. Many fell dead, all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech stayed in Arumah, and Zebul [?] drove out Gaal and his brothers so that they could not live in Shechem.
The next day, the people went out into the open country, and Abimelech was told.
He took his people, divided them into three companies, and they lay in ambush in the open country. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he rose against them and killed them.
Abimelech and the companies with him advanced and took their stand at the entrance of the city gate. The two companies advanced against everyone in the open country and killed them.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed all the people in it. He demolished the city and sowed it with salt.
All the leaders of the tower of Shechem heard about it and came to the stronghold of the temple of El-berith.
Abimelech was told that the leaders of the Tower of Shechem had gathered together.

Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon with all the people who were with him. Abimelech took an ax in his hand, cut off a tree branch, lifted it, and put it on his shoulder. He said to the people with him, “What you have seen me do, hurry and do yourselves, just as I have.”

Each man cut off his own branch, and they followed Abimelech. They piled up the brushwood and burned the city with fire. Everyone in the Tower of Shechem died in the fire, about a thousand men and women altogether.
Abimelech went to Thebez, laid siege to Thebez, and captured it.
There was a strong tower inside the city. All the men and women and all the city's leaders fled there, shut themselves in, and went up onto the roof of the tower.
Abimelech reached the tower and fought against it. He approached the tower's entrance to burn it with fire.
A woman threw a piece of an upper millstone onto Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.

He hurriedly called the young man who carried his weapons and said to him, “Draw your sword and kill me with it, so that they will not say about me, ‘A woman killed him.’” The young man stabbed him, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, each went home.
God repaid Abimelech for the evil he had done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God brought back upon their own heads all the evil that the men of Shechem had done, and the whole curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal [?] came upon them.
After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, arose to deliver Israel. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.
After him Jair the Gileadite arose and judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkey colts. They had thirty towns, which are called the villages of Jair to this day, in the land of Gilead.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

The Israelites again did what was evil before the LORD. They worshiped Baal and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Edom, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, the gods of the Philistines, and the gods of the other nations. They abandoned the LORD and did not worship him.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he handed them over to the Philistines and the Ammonites.
From that year onward they oppressed and afflicted the Israelites for eighteen years—all the Israelites beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Amorites in Gilead.
The Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah and also against the people of Ephraim and Benjamin. Israel was in great distress.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD, saying, “We have sinned against you, for we have abandoned our God and worshiped Baal.”
The LORD said to the Israelites, “Did not the Egyptians, the Moabites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines,
the Sidonians, Amalek, and Ammon oppress you? You cried out to me, and I rescued you from their hands.
But you abandoned me and worshiped other gods. Therefore I will not rescue you again.”
“Go and pray to the gods you have chosen. Let them be your rescuers in the time of your distress.”
The Israelites said to the LORD, “We have sinned against you. Do to us whatever seems good to you; only deliver us today.”
The Israelites removed the foreign gods from among them and worshiped the LORD, because Israel was deeply distressed.
The Ammonites gathered and camped in Gilead. The Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The people, the leaders of Gilead, said to one another, “Whoever begins the fight against the Ammonites will be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was Jephthah's father.
Gilead's wife bore him sons. When his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out, saying, “He shall not inherit our father's house, because he is the son of another woman.”
Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. Worthless men gathered around Jephthah and went out with him.
After some time, the Ammonites fought against the Israelites.
When the Ammonites fought against the Israelites, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.
They said to Jephthah, “Come, be our leader, and let us fight against the Ammonites.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father’s house? Why have you come to me now, when you are in distress?”
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “That is why we have now come to you. Go with us, and let us fight against the Ammonites, and be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “If you bring me back to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD hands them over to me, will I be your head?”
The elders of Gilead said to him, “May the LORD be witness between us if we do not do as you say.”
Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and they appointed him head and ruler over them. Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites to say to him, “What is there between you and me, that you have come to fight in my land?”

The king of the Ammonites said to Jephthah’s messengers, “Because the Israelites took my land when they came up from the land of Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and as far as the Jordan. Now return it to me peacefully.”
Jephthah again sent a letter and messengers to the king of the Ammonites.
He said to him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
For when they came up from Egypt, the Israelites traveled through the wilderness as far as the Sea of Reeds and reached Rekem.

Israel had sent messengers to the king of Edom to say to him, “Let us pass through your land.” But the king of Edom would not listen. Israel also sent word to the king of Moab, but he would not consent, and Israel stayed in Rekem.
Israel traveled through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab. They camped beyond the Arnon and did not enter Moab’s territory, because the Arnon was Moab’s boundary.
Israel had sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites and king of Heshbon. Israel said to him, ‘Let us pass through your land to reach my land.’
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. Sihon gathered all his people, and they camped at Jahaz, and he fought against Israel.
The Lord our God handed Sihon and all his people over to Israel, and Israel destroyed the land of the Amorites.
Israel took possession of all their territory, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now the Lord God has destroyed the Amorites before his people Israel, and are you going to take possession of their territory?
Do you not take possession of whatever Chemosh your god gives you to possess? Whatever the Lord our God destroys before us, that is what we possess.
Now, are you really better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel or fight against them?
While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon for three hundred years, why did you not take them away during that time?
But I have not wronged you now. You are doing me wrong by fighting against me. May the Lord judge today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.”
But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words Jephthah sent him.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh and went on to Mizpah of Gilead. From Mizpah of Gilead he advanced against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the Lord and said, “If you will indeed hand the Ammonites over to me,
whoever comes out of the door of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites will belong to the Lord, and I will offer that person as a burnt offering.”
Jephthah advanced against the Ammonites to fight them, and the Lord handed them over to him.
He struck them down from Aroer as far as the approach to Machir—twenty towns—and as far as Abel-keramim, inflicting a very great defeat. The Ammonites were crushed before the Israelites.
Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah, and there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and timbrels. She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Oh, my daughter! You have utterly brought me down! Today you have become one of those who bring me down, for I have opened my mouth to God, and I cannot take it back.”
His daughter said to him, “My father, you have opened your mouth to God. Do to me what you have said, since the Lord has given you vengeance against your enemies, the Ammonites.”
She said to her father, “Only do this for me: leave me alone for two months, so that I may go and wander over the mountains and weep over my virginity, I and my companions.”
He said to her, “Go,” and sent her away for two months. She went with her companions and wept over her virginity on the mountains.
After two months she returned to her father, and he did to her according to the vow he had made. No man had known her. This became a sign for him among the Israelites.
From time to time, the daughters of Israel would go and weep and mourn for the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite, four days each year.

The men of Ephraim cried out, crossed over to the north, and said to Jephthah, “Why did you cross over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down over you.”
Jephthah said to them, “Men, my people and I were in conflict with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not rescue me from their hands.

When I saw that there was no one to rescue me, I put my life in my own arms and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the Lord delivered them into my hands. Now why have you come up against me today to fight me?”

Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck down the men of Ephraim, because they said that they were Ephraimites, of the house of Ephraim and Manasseh.
The Gileadites seized the Jordan crossing belonging to Ephraim. Whenever those escaping from Ephraim came to the crossing to cross over, the men of Gilead would ask each one, “Are you an Ephraimite?”

He would say, “No.” They would say to him, “Say ‘Shibboleth.’” He would say “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce it that way. They took him across and slaughtered him at the crossing of the Jordan. At that time, forty-two thousand from Ephraim fell.
Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in a town of Gilead.
After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He married his thirty daughters outside the family and brought in thirty daughters-in-law from outside. He judged Israel for seven years.
Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon of Zebulun judged Israel for ten years.
Elon of Zebulun died and was buried in Aijalon, in the land of Zebulun.
After him, Akran son of Helin, the Pirathonite, judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode seventy young donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.
Abdon [?] son of Hillel [?], the Pirathonite, died and was buried in Pirathon, in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
The Israelites again did what was evil before the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, from the tribe of Dan, whose name was Manoah. His wife was barren and had borne no children.
The angel of the Lord appeared to the woman and said to her, “Look, you are barren and have not borne children. Now you will conceive and bear a son.”
“Be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.”

“For look, you will conceive and bear a son. No razor is to touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb. He will begin to rescue Israel from the hands of the Philistines.”

The woman came and told her husband, “A man of God came to me and appeared to me with the appearance of an angel of God, and I was very frightened. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name.

He said to me, ‘Look, you will conceive and bear a son. From now on, do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite dedicated to God from the womb until the day he dies.’”
Manoah prayed to the Lord and said, “Please, Lord, let the man of God whom you sent come to us again and teach us what we should do for the boy who is to be born.”
The Lord listened to Manoah, and the angel of the Lord came again to the woman while she was sitting in the field. Her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman hurried and ran to tell her husband. She said to him, “Look, the man who came to me that day has appeared to me.”
Manoah got up and went with his wife. He came to the man and said to him, “Are you the man who spoke with this woman?”
He said, “I am.” Manoah said, “Now let your word come true. Tell me, what rules should govern the boy, and what is he to do?”
The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “She must be careful about everything I told the woman.
She must not eat anything that comes from the grapevine, drink wine or strong drink, or eat anything unclean. She must observe everything I commanded her.
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “Let us keep you here and prepare a young goat for you.”

The angel of the Lord said to Manoah, “Even if you keep me here, I will not eat your food. If you offer a burnt offering, offer it to the Lord.” For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to the angel of the Lord, “What is your name, so that when your word comes true, we may call on you?”
The angel of the Lord said to him, “Why do you ask about my name? It is glorious.”
Manoah took a young goat and fine flour and offered them on the rock to the Lord. He was praising the Lord, while Manoah and his wife watched.
As the flame of fire rose from the rock toward heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame of the altar. Manoah and his wife saw this, fell with their faces to the ground, and worshiped.
The angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah or his wife. Then Manoah and his wife knew that he was the angel of the Lord.
Manoah said to his wife, “We will certainly die, because we have seen God.”

His wife said to him, “If God had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and fine flour from us. Nor would he have shown us all these things at this time or told us these things.”
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
The Spirit of the Lord began to move him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a woman there from among the Philistine women.
He went up and told his father and mother, “I saw a woman in Timnah from among the Philistine women. Now get her for me as a wife.”

His father and mother said to him, “Is there no woman here in your father’s family or among all your people, that you are going to take a wife from among the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, because she pleases me.”
His father and mother did not know that this was from the Lord, so that redress might be sought from the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they reached the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion came roaring toward him.
The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and he tore the lion apart as someone would tear apart a young goat, though he had nothing in his hand. He did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
They went down and spoke with the woman, and she pleased Samson.
After some days he returned to marry her. He turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass, and there was a swarm of bees in the lion’s body.
He scooped honey into his hands and walked on to his father and mother. He gave them some, and they ate it, but he did not tell them that he had scooped the honey from the lion’s body.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson held a feast there for seven days, because that was how warriors held a feast.
When they saw him, thirty men came and became his wedding companions.
Samson said to them, “Let me tell you a riddle. If you can explain it to me during the seven days of the feast and discover its meaning, I will give you thirty tunics and thirty sets of clothes.
But if you cannot explain it to me, you must give me thirty tunics and thirty sets of clothes.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle, and let us hear it.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came food, and out of the bitter came sweetness.” They could not solve the riddle for three days.
On the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Persuade your husband to tell us his riddle, or we will burn you and your father’s household with fire and take possession of his inheritance.”

Samson’s wife wept and said to him, “You certainly hate me and do not love me, because you have not told me the riddle you posed to my people.” He said to her, “I have not told my father or my mother. Should I tell you?”
She wept during those seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she had pressured him, and she revealed the riddle to her people.

On the seventh day, before the [?] began, the men of the town said, “What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” Samson said to them, “If you had not coaxed my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle.”

The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon him. He went down to Ashkelon, seized thirty men from among them, killed them, took their clothes, and gave them to those who had solved his riddle. His anger flared up, and he went up to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife, whom he loved, became the wife of his best man.
Some time later, during the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. He said, “I will go to my wife in her room.” But her father would not let him enter.
Her father said, “I thought you thoroughly hated her, so I gave her to your best man. Look, her younger sister is better than she is. Let her be yours instead.”
Samson said to them, “I am free of blame toward the Philistines for the harm I am doing to you.”
Samson went and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches and tied the foxes together in pairs by their tails. He tied one torch between each pair of foxes, between their two tails.

He set fire to the torches and released the foxes into the Philistines’ standing grain. He burned everything from the heaps of harvested grain to the standing grain, the vineyards, and the olive trees.

The Philistines asked, “Who did this?” They were told, “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite [?], because he took Samson’s wife and gave her to his best man.” So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father’s household with fire.
Samson said to them, “Even if you do this, I will take revenge on you, and then I will stop.”
He struck them from their legs to their hips, inflicting a great slaughter. Then he went and stayed in the cleft in the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah.
The men of Judah asked, “Why have you come up?” They said, “We have come up to bind Samson and do to him as he did to us.”

Three thousand men from Judah went down to the cleft in the rock of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?” He said to them, “I did to them just as they did to me.”
They said to him, “We have come down to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.” He said to them, “Swear to me that you yourselves will not attack me.”
They said to him, “No, we will only bind you and hand you over to them. We certainly will not kill you.” They bound him with two new chains and brought him up from the rock.
When he reached Lehi, the Philistines rose to kill him. The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and the chains on his arms became like flax scorched by fire. His bonds came loose from his hands.
He found a fresh donkey’s jawbone, reached out his hand and took it, and killed a thousand men with it.
Samson said, “With a donkey’s jawbone I have piled them in heaps. With a donkey’s jawbone I have killed a thousand men.”
When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand and named that place Blood of the Jawbone.

He became very thirsty and called to the Lord, saying, “You have given this great victory through the hand of your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of these uncircumcised men?”

The Lord God split open the hollow in the donkey’s jawbone, and water came out of it. He drank, and his spirit revived. Therefore he named that place Spring of the Horn of the Donkey’s Jawbone, as it is called to this day.
He judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson went to Gaza, saw a prostitute there, and went in to her.
Word reached Gaza that Samson had come there. They lay in ambush for him all night at the city gate. They whispered all night, saying, “When morning dawns, we will kill him.”

Samson slept until midnight. At midnight he got up, took hold of the two posts of the city gate, and pulled it up along with its fastenings. He put it on his shoulder and carried them up to the hill opposite Hebron.
Afterward he fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah.

The rulers of the Philistines came up to her and said, “Persuade him and find out what makes his strength so great, and how we can overpower him and bind him to subdue him. Each of us will give you thirteen hundred pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me what makes your strength so great, how you can be bound, and whether you can be weakened.”
Samson said to her, “If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not dried, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
The rulers of the Philistines brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not dried, and she bound him with them.

She had men lying in ambush in the room. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He snapped the bowstrings as a flax thread snaps when fire touches it, and his strength was not shaken.
Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have deceived me and told me lies. Tell me how you can be bound.”
He said to her, “If they bind me securely with new chains that have never been used for any work, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
Delilah took new chains and bound him with them. She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” She had men lying in ambush in the room, but he snapped the chains off his arms like thread.
Delilah said to Samson, “Look, you have deceived me and told me lies. Tell me how you can be bound.” He said to her, “If you weave the seven locks of hair on my head into the woven fabric.”
She wove them into the loom and said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and pulled up the weaver’s loom along with the woven fabric.
She said to him, “How can you tell me, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? You have deceived me these three times and have not told me what makes your strength so great.”
She distressed him with her words every day and kept pressing him until he was troubled to the point of death.

He revealed everything in his heart to her and said, “No razor has touched my head, because I have been a Nazirite dedicated to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like everyone else.”

When Delilah saw that he had revealed everything in his heart to her, she sent for the rulers of the Philistines, saying, “Come up now, because he has revealed everything in his heart to me.” The rulers of the Philistines came up to her, bringing the silver with them.
She put him to sleep on her knees, called for a barber, and shaved off the seven locks of hair on his head. She began to subdue him, and his strength left him.
She said to him, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He awoke from his sleep and said, “I will go out as I always do and shake them off.” But he did not know that the Lord had left him.
The Philistines seized him, put out his eyes, bound him with chains, and brought him down to Gaza. He worked at grinding in the prison.
The hair on his head began to grow again after he had been shaved.
The rulers of the Philistines gathered joyfully to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god. They said, “Our god has handed Samson our enemy over to us.”
When they saw him, they praised their god, saying, “Our god has handed over to us our enemy, who devastated our lands and killed so many of us.”
When they were in good spirits, they said, “Call Samson to dance before us.” They called Samson out of the prison, and he danced before them. They placed him between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy who was holding his hand, “Let me go, and let me feel the pillars that support the house, so I can lean against them.”
The building was full of men and women, and all the rulers of the Philistines were there. On the roof were about three thousand men and women, watching Samson as he danced.
Samson called to the Lord and said, “Please, Lord God, remember me and strengthen me just this once, God, so that I can take revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson grasped the two middle pillars that supported the house and leaned against them, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He pulled with all his strength, and the house fell on the rulers and all the people inside it. Those who died at Samson’s death were more numerous than those who died during his life.
All his brothers and his father’s entire household went down, brought him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you pronounced a curse that I myself heard—you have spoken about that silver in my hearing. I took it.” His mother said, “May my son be blessed by the Lord!”

He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. His mother said, “I have solemnly dedicated the silver from my own hands to the Lord, my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. Now return it to me.”
He returned the silver to his mother, and his mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to the metalworker. He made a carved image and a cast image, and it was placed in Micah’s house.
This man Micah had a house of God. He made an ephod and a curtain, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah whose name was Levi, and he lived there.
The man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to live wherever he could find a place. As he traveled, he reached the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house.
Micah said to him, “Where are you coming from?” He answered, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to live wherever I can find a place.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me and be like a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, as well as your clothing and food.” And Levi went.
He agreed to stay with the man, and the young man became like one of his sons.
Micah ordained the Levite, and he became his priest and lived in Micah’s house.
Micah said, “Now I know that the Lord will be good to me, because I have a Levite as my priest.”
In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of Dan was seeking territory to settle in, because up to that day no inheritance had been allotted to it among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites sent five men from their clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and investigate it. They told them, “Go and investigate the land.” They came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah’s house, and spent the night there.
While they were at Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young man Levi. They turned aside to him there and said to him, “Why have you come here, and what are you doing here?”
He told them, “Micah has done such and such for me. He hired me, and I became his priest.”
They said to him, “Please consult God for us, so we may know whether the journey we are making will succeed.”
The priest told them, “Go in peace, and may the Lord make straight the path you are taking.”

The five men went to Laish and saw that the people living there lived quietly, following the custom of the Sidonians, peaceful and untroubled. There was no one in the land to terrorize them, nor anyone to oppress or trouble them. They were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
They came to their fellow Israelites at Zorah and Eshtaol, and their fellow Israelites asked them, “Where have you come from?”
They said, “From Laish. Come, let us go up against them now, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Do not remain silent or be reluctant to go, enter, and take possession of the land.
When you enter their territory, you will come upon a prosperous people and a land stretching wide before you, because God has delivered it into your hands. You will lack nothing in the land.”
Then six hundred men from the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol.
They went up and camped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why that place is called the Camp of Dan to this day. It is behind Kiriath-jearim.
From there they passed into the hill country of Ephraim and went as far as Micah’s house.

The five men who had gone to explore the land of Laish spoke up and said to their fellow Israelites, “Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, teraphim, a carved image, and a cast image? Now consider what you should do.”
They turned aside and entered the young Levite’s house, at Micah’s house, and greeted him.
The six hundred Danite men, armed with weapons of war, stood at the entrance to the gate.

The five men who had gone to explore the land went up, entered there, and took the image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the cast image, while the priest stood at the entrance to the gate with those six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
They entered Micah’s house and took the image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the cast image. The priest said to them, “What are you doing?”

They said to him, “Be quiet. Put your hand over your mouth and come with us. Be a father and a priest to us. Which is better for you: to be a priest to one man’s household, or to be a priest to a clan and a tribe of Israel?”
The priest was pleased. He took the image, the ephod, and the [?], and went with the people.
They turned and continued on their way, with the women, possessions, and livestock ahead of them.
They had gone some distance from Micah’s house, and the man who was in the house beside Micah’s house cried out and pursued the Danites.
He called out to the Danites, and they turned and said to Micah, “What is wrong with you, that you are shouting?”
He said to them, “You have taken the god I made, taken the priest as well, and gone away. What do I have left? Yet you ask me, ‘What is wrong with you?’”
The Danites said to him, “Do not let us hear your voice, or some angry men may attack you, and you and your sons will lose your lives.”
The Danites went on their way. When Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, he turned back and went home.
They took what Micah had made and took away the priest he had. They entered Laish and attacked a prosperous and peaceful people. They struck them down with the sword and burned the city.
There was no one to rescue them, because it was far from Sidon and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley of Beth-rehob. They rebuilt the city and settled in it.
They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. Previously, however, the city’s name was Luz.
The Danites set up the image for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the day the land was taken into captivity.
They set up for themselves Micah’s image, which they had made, for as long as the house of God was in Shiloh.
In those days there was no king in Israel. There was a Levite living in the foothills of the hill country, and he took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
His concubine was unfaithful to him. She got up and left him for her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah, and she stayed there for four months.

Her husband got up and went after her to speak to her heart and bring her back. His servant and two donkeys were with him. She brought him into her father’s house, and the young woman’s father saw him and welcomed him gladly.
His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, persuaded him to stay, and he stayed with him for three days. They ate, drank, and spent the nights there.
On the fourth day he rose early in the morning to leave. The young woman’s father said to his son-in-law, “Strengthen yourself with a piece of bread, and then you can get up and go.”
The two of them sat down together and ate and drank. The young woman's father said to his son-in-law, “If you wish, stay the night and enjoy yourself.”
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him to stay, so he spent the night there.

On the fifth day he rose early in the morning to leave. The young woman's father said to him, “Have something to eat to strengthen yourself, and stay until the day declines.” So the two of them ate and drank.

The man got up to leave with his concubine and his servant. His father-in-law, the young woman's father, said to him, “Look, the day is drawing to a close. Stay here tonight and enjoy yourself. Get up early tomorrow and go home.”
But the man was unwilling to stay the night. He got up and left and came opposite Jebus, which is Jerusalem. He had two loaded donkeys with him, and his concubine was with him.
They were near Jebus, and the day was far spent. The servant said to his master, “Come, let us turn aside into this town of Jebus and spend the night there.”
His master said to him, “We will not turn aside into a foreign town that does not belong to the Israelites. Instead, we will go on to Gibeah.”
His master said to him, “Come, let us make our way to one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.”
They continued on their way, and the sun set as they were near Gibeah in Benjamin.
They turned aside there to spend the night and entered Gibeah. They sat down in the town square, but no one took them into a house for the night.

Then an old man came in that evening from his work in the field. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah in Benjamin. The local people were Benjaminites, and their deeds were very wicked.
The old man looked up and saw the traveler in the town square. The old man said to him, “Where are you going, and where have you come from?”

He said to him, “We are passing through from Bethlehem in Judah to the slopes of the hill country. I am from there, and I went to Bethlehem in Judah. I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken us into a house.
We have both straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, for your maidservant, and for the young man, your servant. We lack nothing.”
The old man said to him, “Peace to you! I will provide whatever you need. Just do not spend the night in the square.”
He brought him into his house and gave his donkey feed. They washed their feet and ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, some men of the town, wicked men, surrounded the house and pounded on the door. They said to the old man who owned the house, “Bring out the man who came into your house so that we can have sex with him.”
The old man who owned the house went out to them and said, “No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. Since this man has come into my house, do not do this disgraceful thing.
Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out. Humiliate them and do whatever you please, but do not do this disgraceful thing to this man.”
But those men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and brought her outside to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and they let her go when dawn broke.
The woman came at daybreak and fell at the doorway of the man’s house where her master was, and remained there until it was light.
Her master got up in the morning, opened the door of the house, and went out to continue on his way. He saw his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hand on the doorway.
He said to her, “Get up, and let us go.” But she did not answer him. He lifted her onto his donkey, and the man got up and went home.
He entered his house, took a knife, and cut his concubine into twelve pieces. He sent them throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who saw her said, “Nothing like this has happened or been seen from the day the Israelites came up from the land of Egypt until today. Consider it, take counsel, and speak!”
All the Israelites came out, and the entire assembly gathered as one man, from Dan to Beersheba and the land of Gilead, before the LORD at Mizpah.
The clans of all the people, all the tribes of Israel, took their places in the assembly of God's people: four hundred thousand foot soldiers armed with swords.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, “Tell us how this evil happened.”
The Levite, the husband of the woman who had been killed, answered them, “My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house where I was during the night. They wanted to kill me, and they abused my concubine, and she died.
